speechtext: The House resumed from Wednesday, May 16, the debate on the motion of Hon. W. S. Fielding (Minister of Finance) that Mr. Speaker do now leave the chair for the House to go into Committee of Ways and Means, and the proposed amendment thereto of Mr. Robert Forke.

subtopic: CONTINUATION OF DEBATE ON THE ANNUAL FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I find the most difficult part of making a speech in this House is to get started; and I notice that some members find it equally difficult to stop. The budget speech may be described as the chief event of the session. A great deal of interest is always taken in it not only by hon. members but by the people generally, for it deals with taxation and debt. Once you touch the pockets of the people you instantly arouse a good deal of criticism and opposition, and I do not think that any man in this House or outside knows more about that feature of a budget than the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding).
The present budget appears to me to be drafted not so much for the purpose of meeting the exigencies of the national situation as for its political effect. It is a colourless and featureless budget devoid of any outstanding characteristics. The hon. Minister of Finance last week presented his seventeenth budget, a record in our parliamentary history, and I compliment him on his long and useful service to the country. The hon. gentleman, previous to the election of 1896 was an
The Budget-Mr. Anderson

advocate of free trade or tariff for revenue, but during the following fifteen years while in power, he made no effort to implement his promises, and the people watched in vain for some signs that he remembered his promises. In 1911 he asked the approval of the country of a reciprocity pact with the United States, but the people would have none of it. That is a matter of history. But now, in 1923, after the country had spoken so emphatically on that question in 1911, he comes back with a resolution for the same purpose.
The hon. gentleman has been either a free trader or an advocate of a tariff for revenue all the time he was in opposition, but in power he has always been a protectionist. It would be interesting, Mr. Speaker, to know what are the reasons that cause this sudden change of front when he succeeds to office. What caused his change of front in 1896, and again in 1921? Are we to believe that the hon. Minister of Finance was not sincere in his demands for a tariff for revenue when he was in oppostiion? Was his change of front due to a fear on his part that such a policy would not be in the best interests of the country? Did he fear that such a policy would not be in the best interests of the party in which he occupies such a prominent position? During the Liberal regime of 1896 to 1911, a period of 15 years, the Liberal government reduced the average rate of tariff duties by the small amount of 79/100 of one per cent. That statement was made in this House a few years ago by the then member for Red Deer Dr. Clark. Dr. Clark evidently knew what he was talking about when he made that statement, because he was a member of the Liberal party. That was the full extent to which the Liberal party ventured into the charmed field of free trade. Evidently when they get into office it does not present a pleasing view to them; and it is less pleasing now, for since they came into office, instead of reducing the average tariff duties they increased them in the year 192223 by 74/100 of one per cent over what they were in 1921. This is a peculiar way to lower tariff duties, to get down to a tariff for revenue purposes only or to a free trade policy. I cannot say that I blame the Finance Minister for this. I believe in the principle of protection-a moderate protection, not a high protection-and believing in that I cannot blame the minister for not reducing the tariff duties. The figures upon which I base this statement are the following: In the first eleven months of 1921-22, ending February 28, 1922-I am taking the eleven months be-
IMt. Anderson.]
cause' at the time I made the calculation the figures for the whole year were not available -the amount of dutiable goods imported for home consumption was $422,309,490. The duty collected was $107,186,255, making an average rate of duty on all dutiable articles of 24-23 per cent. In the first eleven months of 1922-23, ending February 28, 1923, the amount of dutiable goods imported for home consumption was $475,583,587, on which the duty collected was $118,872,102, making an average duty of 24-97 per cent and showing an increase over 1921-22 of -74 per cent. The total merchandise dutiable and free imported in the same period-and I am making the calculation on the basis of all articles imported, whether there was duty collected on them or not-amounted to $668,425,606 on which was collected for duty purposes $107,186,255, the amount which I have already mentioned, showing an average rate of duty on all goods of 16 -34 per cent. For the eleven months period in 1922-23 there were imported $710,583,616 worth of goods dutiable and free, on which was collected $118,872,102, showing an average duty of 16-81 per cent, or *34 per cent higher than it was in 1921. I am just bringing these facts to the attention of the House to show how far the Minister of Finance and the Liberal party have kept their promises to the people to reduce the duties on imported goods. Instead of reducing them, on the average they have raised them. I could give the figures for the whole year, having received them subsequent to making these calculations, but I think it is unnecessary to do so.
I may say that the Minister of Finance is now firmly entrenched in the National Policy of Sir John A. Macdonald. After seventeen years during which the Finance Minister was pledged to a tariff for revenue he comes down this year with the statement that he believes in the principle of protection and that the tariff of Sir John A. Macdonald of 1878 is good enough for him. In making the statement that he could not further reduce the tariff duties he practically accepted the principle of pro tection. The principle of protection is the real essence of the National Policy of 1878. That National Policy was introduced not with the idea of its standing always as a moderate or a high protective policy; It was introduced a:' a protective policy, and when the hon. Minister of Finance accepts that policy to-day he accepts in his financial affairs the principle of protection. Having posed all these years as being in favour of a tariff for revenue, in 1923 he changes by one touch of his magic

The Budget-Mr. Anderson
hand the high protective policy of Sir John A. Macdonald into a moderate tariff policy a policy which hon. gentlemen now on the government benches designated as a high protective tariff while in opposition. A tariff "in favour of the big interests," a tariff that "imposed intolerable burdens on the people," a tariff which he pledged himself and his party to do away with when elected to office, has been changed over night by his magic touch into a tariff for revenue.
The hon. Minister of Finance is not the only convert to the principle of protection I must compliment the right hon. leader of the Opposition on the efficiency he has shown in making converts, because it is largely due to him that these conversions have been taking place. The hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) only a few days ago in his statement expressed the opinion that the protective principle was all right. I understood him to say that a tariff for revenue was impossible without a certain measure of protection, that is, that there is an incidental measure of protection, in any tariff for revenue purposes. The hon. Minister of Agriculture has not thoroughly studied the question or he would not have made such a statement. It is not in accordance with the facts and with experience. The British Government only a couple of years ago collected over 8600,000,000 in duties without giving any incidental protection. Those duties were placed upon articles which they did not produce at home.

There was nobody to
protect. Nobody was producing the article, consequently no measure of incidental protection was given to the English people. Perhaps what the minister meant when he made that statement was that he could get away from the protective principle by having an excise duty on the articles which we produce. He could offset the protective principle in the tariff by putting on an excise duty equal to the import duty on the article in question, but I cannot see where or in what way that would reduce the cost of living to any people. The Minister of Finance in his budget speech last year said that he intended to make such adjustments in the tariff itself as would so far as possible reduce the cost of living, and he did last year make an attempt at
that by reducing the protective duty on farm implements by two and one-half per cent. But in lieu of that he added a two per cent excise tax. The result was that the cost of the imported article remained practically the same and the home-made article was raised by two per cent. The farmer got absolutely no advantage from it. You cannot reduce the cost of living by an excise tax.
The hon. Minister of Immigration and Colonization (Mr. Stewart) would appear to me to be a convert to the principle of protection. He said in his speech yesterday:
I do not believe, and I have had nothing to convince me, that so heavy a rate of protection is required as is given to many of the industries existent in this country to-day.
The minister does not oppose the principle of protection; he is simply opposed to high protection, and thus protection is being kept in force apparently with the connivance of the Minister of Immigration and Colonization. The Minister of Finance in his want of confidence motion on the budget of 1921 made this statement:
The tariff is a tax, and the aim of legislation should be to make taxation as light as circumstances will permit.
I do not dispute that statement. I think it should be the object of legislation to make the cost of living as light as possible. The Minister of Finance implemented that by stating he would make an effort to reduce the cost of living. Now, Mr. Speaker, the tariff is certainly a tax, and a tax on somebody; there may be some dispute at times as to who pays the tariff tax, but certainly there can be no dispute as to who pays an excise tax. An excise tax is a home tax. It is placed on the commodities in the country itself. There is nobody but the Canadian people to pay it. But when an article is imported into this country there may be cases in which the exporter of the article, that is the producer in a foreign country may pay all or part of the duty. Who pays the tax on articles that are dumped into this country at prices lower than the cost of production in the country of origin? It may not be the consumer in this country. Possibly it is the manufacturer or producer of the article in the foreign country. There may be some question about that, but there can be no question about who pays an excise tax.
With regard to the sales tax, no matter what can be said in regard to its being a means of increasing the revenue, it directly and immediately is reflected in an increased cost to the Canadian people of the articles on which the duty is placed. It has an im-
The Budget-Mr. Anderson

mediate effect. It does increase the price of that article. A larger amount of revenue is collected from the people, and the manufacturer or the dealer passes on the tax to the consumer. If he has a narrow margin of profit he must do that or go out of business. The sales tax can have no other effect but to increase the cost of living to every Canadian. So long as the need of taxation exists, so long as a large revenue is necessary to earn- on the business of this country, a sales tax judiciously applied is a very efficient tax. I consider that it is a just tax because the average individual will pay the tax in proportion to his ability to purchase. The more wealthy he is the more he will purchase and the more taxation he will pay. I can have no objection to that tax.
There is, however, one feature about the present increase in the tax to six per cent to which I would refer. I would think that a tax at the fountain source is perhaps the best way of collecting it, and I commend the Minister of Finance for making the change. Last year instead of changing the application of the tax he increased it by fifty per cent. I want to show by some figures I have that that was immediately reflected in the returns of the Excise department, and in connection with these returns I want to emphasize the fact that as the tax was collected entirely from the Canadian people it must and did result in an increased cost of living. I remind the House that this tax came into force on the 23rd of May, 1922. The revenue from the sales tax for April, 1922, was $2,072,000. The average amount collected for the previous four months-I did not think it was fair to take only April, because it may have been smaller than the other months, so I took the average collections from the domestic sales tax for the months of January, February, March and April, 1922-was $3,-
126,000.	Hon. gentlemen will notice that in May-and remember, the tax only came into force on the 23rd of May-there was a decided increase, in sales tax collections. Here are the figures:

The revenue was necessary; I am in no way criticizing the Minister of Finance for having asked the people to contribute it.	I am only saying, that by increasing the sales tax in order to add to the revenue he was not adopting the most satisfactory way of reducing the cost of living. It had not the effect which he intended; as a matter of fact, the result was the opposite. The decision to levy the sales tax of 6 per cent at the source of production of the article is wise, I believe. There may be some difficulty in deciding just where is the fountain source of the finished articles, for what is the finished article to one manufacturer may be the raw material to another. I believe the Minister of Finance will experience considerable difficulty in coming to a conclusion as to where the tax should be levied. No doubt a committee will be appointed, or possibly the department will itself undertake to settle this matter, and I presume that regulations will be made to ensure that the tax shall not be collected more than once. That was the fault in connection with the previous tax of \\ per cent, for I believe that in many instances it was collected several times, probably three or four times

The Budget-Mr. Anderson
over; at any rate, in certain instances it was as high as 15 or 20 per cent of the cost of the article. I hope that the minister will devise some means of preventing this repetition of payment in connection with the present 0 per cent tax.	.
In regard to the question of deciding upon the origin of a finished article, in the manner of clothing or of a cloth, for example, I do not know how the minister will settle the point as to who is the manufacturer. Will it be the tailor, the retail man who makes the clothes, or will it be the manufacturer who produces the cloth? These are difficulties which I have no doubt can be overcome, but I have certain criticism of the question.
Many manufacturers as well as men of business have stated that a turnover tax would be more satisfactory than the sales tax. It is possible that a turnover tax might be more advantageous, because the man who had large profits would pay a greater proportion of it. He would not be so apt to pass it on to the consumer; he could absorb it into his business. I think that this suggestion in regard to a turnover tax might well receive the consideration of the Minister of Finance in the future.
There is one particular article on which the sales tax was placed last year in regard to w'hich some modification would be advisable. As I have previously stated, I am not a high protectionist, and I think there are some industries in this country which possibly are too highly protected. One of these, I think, is the automobile industry. This industry is making rapid strides in Canada and in the last year this country, a country of nine million people, exported half as many automobiles as did the United States, with a population of 110,000,000. This shows that the industry is flourishing in this country. There is a duty of 35 per cent on the imported car, and to that was added last year a sales tax of 10 per cent. I did not understand from the Minister of Finance whether he intended to abolish that tax or not; I think it has been reduced to 6 per cent; that at least is my understanding of the matter. When an automobile is introduced into this country a 5 per cent charge is made on it over the sales price in the United States; to that there is added 35 per cent of a duty collected in Canada; and on top of that was the 10 per cent sales tax, making something like 52 per cent of the cost price on the American side which was charged to the purchaser here. That is too great protection, and I think that the minister might have left off the 10
per cent sales tax on the imported car and brought the protection down to 25 per cent.
Now, the Minister of Finance has not only come over as a convert, to the protective principle in our policy, but he has repudiated the whole Liberal platform of 1919. In his speech in the by-election at Windsor on February 27, he made this statement, speaking on the subject of the Liberal platform of 1919:
That is not the policy on which I appealed to the country.
I only wish the Minister of Finance were in his place; I would ask him why he used the pronoun "I." I do not know whether he meant to imply that his personal policy was different from that of the Liberal party. However, he went on to say:
And that policy was never endorsed by the Liberal party after it got into power.
Well, we know that it was not; that was undoubtedly a truism. The Liberal party never endorsed their policy after they got into power; they used it mereW for the purpose of getting into power, and it was a dead letter after they assumed office. Now the Minister of Finance repudiates it altogether. He said that he never at any time promised to endorse it.
Now I come to the question of the finality of the minister's budget, regarding the tariff. There is some doubt as to whether the minister really intimated that we had reached bottom in the reductions in the tariff. Evidently the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) does not believe that we have, because in the course of his speech in this House the other day he made a very significant remark. I will quote his words:
Who said this was the last word?-
Meaning the statement of the Minister of Finance that he had reached the final decision with regard to the reductions in the tariff.
Who said this was the last word?. . . . Nobody said it was the last word. The Minister of Finance said distinctly there was no finality, that what parliament did to-day it might undo to-morrow.
Did the Minister of Finance leave a way for retreat from the position he has taken? Is the Minister of Agriculture right in his supposition that his colleague did not mean what he said? The words that the Minister of Finance used in his speech were these:
Speaking broadly, it is possible to give the country a reasonable assurance of stability of tariff.
Now, I believe that the country has a right to accept that statement from the Minister of Finance and to assume that the question of tariff reductions has been settled. It has gone
The Budget-Mr. Anderson

out to the people of the country, particularly those encaged in industry, that the matter has been decided, and the effect of this assurance is to dispose these people to extend their plants and to go further into manufacturing industries.
Coming now to other phases of the budget, let us consider the statement of the Minister of Finance with reft-;trice to the necessity for economy. I think that economy in the government is absolutely necessary. The time has arrived, I think, when revenue might very easily meet expenditure. We should balance our budget and endeavour in addition to have a small surplus with which to start a sinking fund for the purpose of paying off the national debt. If we go on adding to the debt each year the interest charges will increase so that it will become an intolerable burden to the people. Why should we pass that burden on to future generations? We should stand up to our responsibilities and make every effort to meet them as we go along. But the Minister of Finance makes no effort to do this in the present budget ; in fact, he gives us a statement to the very opposite effect, that next year it is possible the revenue will not meet current expenditure and that there will consequently be a further addition to the national debt. I have looked up the national debt of Canada for some years back and I find that in 1867 it was $75,000,000; in 1914, $335,000,000; in 1918, $1,191,000,000; in 1922, $2,422,000,000; in 1923, $2,471,000,000. That is the net debt of the Dominion, and it is still increasing; last year the Minister of Finance added $49,000,000 to it. I had the curosity to look into the current expenditures of previous years; I mean the ordinary expenditures of government, not capital expenditure. I think it is reasonable to take from the expenditures of the present year the amount that is paid in interest on the national debt, increase due to the war. that is, the debt incurred by the war, and that includes the amount paid for pensions and other expenditures in connection with the war.
I have compiled the figures, putting the year 1923 on the same basis as 1913, when there was no war and had not been for some time. The war is now five years behind us. It is that far back in history, and it is time we were getting down to a pre-war level. We are not getting back to pre-war conditions as fast as we might. During the war there were many activities which are not in existence, now. There were many civil servants in the Militia department and other departments that are not needed now. Their services have been dispensed with, and if they had not been dispensed with there would have been a very much greater balance against the present day expenditure. It is all very well for the minister-and I commend him for it-to call upon the people to economize in their private affairs, to get down to practical business by producing more, but the trouble is that the Finance Minister is not setting a good example. He preaches a good doctrine but does not practice it. I think that economy is vitally necessary at the present time in the conduct of affairs by the government. We should endeavour to make ends meet, and establish a sinking fund in order to reduce our debt. We should make an effort to reduce the interest charges year by year. We do not desire large surpluses, Mr. Speaker, but we ought to make the budget balance and provide a few millions for a sinking fund. I think that leadership is needed in the matter of economy, and the present Finance Minister is not giving us that leadership.
The budget speech embodies a resolution offering reciprocity to the United States. Now, we had a reciprocity pact with the United States once before-from 1854 to 1864. Immediately at the end of that period the

The Budget-Mr. Anderson
United States gave notice that they would abrogate that treaty. The treaty was made for a period of ten years, renewable if the contracting parties were agreeable. They abrogated the treaty immediately after the United States Civil War, giving as their reason that they needed a greater revenue, that they needed to restrict imports in order to bring their dollar up to par value, and also that they desired to cultivate industries in their own country and give employment to their own people. At that time, Mr. Speaker, we had made arrangements by which our transportation companies were running north and south in order to take care of the trade which went in those directions. Transportation will follow commerce and possibly commerce will follow transportation, but at any rate we had placed ourselves in such a position that we imported from the United States most of our manufactured commodities, and we looked to the United States for a market for the produce of our farms. The result was that after the Civil war the United States put up a tariff duty against us. We had no tariff duty against the United States, and the consequence was that after 1865 we had the greatest and most serious depression in trade this country has ever experienced. In 1876 it was so serious that parliament appointed a commission to mquire into the problem. And, looking up the history of that time, it seemed peculiar to me that the committee inquiring into those conditions went over to. New York city, and sat there for a considerable time inquiring into the depression in trade conditions in the Dominion of Canada. At that time the treaty was abrogated, and a duty was placed against Canada largely at the instance of the agricultural interests of the United States. History is repeating itself. Although the United States was not interested in the Great War to the extent that we were, immediately after that war the agricultural interests of the United States demanded that, they should have an increased tariff against the imports from the Dominion of Canada. That was acceded to by the United States government, and we have to-day as a result the Fordney Bill which practically prohibits many articles from this country going into the United States. The same conditions prevail now as existed then. The United States, if they were willing to listen to us in 1911 with regard to reciprocity, are not likely to listen to us at the present time, because there is that restraint upon the government, and the agriculturists of that country do not desire reciprocity with Canada. Even if we had a reciprocity agreement at the present time, what would
be the result? Trade undoubtedly would begin to flow to the United States. Our transportation facilities might not be equal to the flow of that trade, and the consequence would be that we would have to change our present transportation system. For a number of years we have had no reciprocity treaty with the United States, and we have our transportation system travelling east and west. We have cultivated an interprovincial trade and also a world trade. I believe that the world market is the one to which we should look to-day, and that we should not confine ourselves entirely to the United States market. It is all right to trade with our neighbours. We are trading more with them than with any other part of the world. I wish to place on Hansard a few figures in connection with that matter. At the present time over 75 per cent of the trade of this country is done with the British Empire and the United States, and not quite 25 per cent of it done with the rest of the world. If they want the wheat of the Canadian west

Just a word or two with regard to immigration, which is an important, subject at the present time. The other day I noticed an article by Sir Henry Thornton. Sir Henry Thornton speaks on many questions, and although possibly he may speak too often, yet his statements in this article are sound indeed. With regard to immigration he said:
Four salient points were emphasized with regard to the immigration problems of Canada by Sir Henry Thornton. . . . First, a capable Minister of Immigration who would co-ordinate all the efforts of the people, is needed.

speechtext:
I think the House
must decide that question; I do not care at the moment to give a decision. Like the hon. Minister of Agriculture, I am not the interpretation clause of the House. I hope my hon. friends to the left will not take it as being discourteous on my part, for it certainly is not so intended, when I attempt to show that the farmers of the prairie provinces financially are as well off as the farmers of the East. We are all suffering more or less from hard times and the people of Ontario are no exception, indeed it is a condition that prevails not only in the western provinces but in the eastern. I had the curiosity to look up a return showing the number of rural income taxpayers in Canada for 1922; these numbered 18,873. In the three prairie provinces, 11,656 rural citizens paid income tax, or 61-75 per cent of the total number, while the rest of Canada accounted for 7,217, or 38-25 per cent. The rural citizens of the three prairie provinces who were able to pay income tax were almost twice as many as those in the rest of Canada. Our western farmers are either better able to pay income tax, that is, they are enjoying larger incomes, or they may be more honest than their rural brothers in the other provinces. Of course, I cannot say as to that. I believe the government is making every possible effort to collect income tax from all who are liable, but I have no doubt many escape payment. Taking the rural income taxpayers in proportion to popu-
The Budget-Mr. Anderson

lation, I find the prairies provinces with a population of 1,252,753 show 1 in every 108 farmers; the rest of Canada with a rural population of 3,770,197 show 1 in every 523 farmers; Ontario with a rural population of 1,226,292 shows 1 in every 200 farmers. In other words in the three prairie provinces they had almost twice as many rural income taxpayers to the population as they had in the province of Ontario, and five times as many as in the rest of the Dominion. That surely is not an index of hard times; it shows that the farmers of the West have money. Taking the figures by provinces they are as follows:
In Saskatchewan, 6,560 in rural population of 538,522- 1 in every 82 farmers.
In Manitoba, 3,458 in rural population of 348,651-

1 in every 223 farmers.
In Quebec, 150 in rural population of 1,038,128-1 in every 6,920 farmers.
In British Columbia 640 in rural population of 272,020-1 in every 425 farmers.
Taking our bank shareholders I find on referring to Hansard that in the rural districts	the	prairie	provinces contain
1,794 out of a total of 3,887 for the whole Dominion, leaving for the rest of Canada 2.093. This means that among the rural population of 1,252,753 in the three prairie provinces one farmer in every 698 is a bank shareholder, while in the rest of Canada with a rural population of 3,770,397 one farmer in every 1,802 is in this happy position, Bhowing again that the rural people of the prairie provinces had more money than their rural friends in the other provinces for investment in bank shares.
Again, take the field crops. I will not go fully into this; it will suffice to say that Canada ranks second in production among the wheat producing countries of the world and third in area, the United States first in production and first in area; India third in production and second in area. The wheat production of the world amounted in 1922 to 3.012,293,000 bushels; the production of Canada was 391,425,000 bushels, and of the United. States 310,123,000 bushels. So that there was an increase in the prairie provinces for those years of $128,000,000 as against a decrease in the rest of Canada of $76,000,000, as I have shown. That does not indicate that there are any harder times in the prairie provinces than there are in the rest of Canada, and I fail to see what basis the Progressives have for the statements they have made in this House, statements which are not in the best interests of the Dominion of Canada and are certainly very detrimental to the West. The rest of Canada has always been friendly to the West. Only a few days ago some of the members of the Progressive party suggested to' me that there was an unfriendly feeling between the East and the West. I cannot undertsand such a statement; there is nothing of the kind. It seems to me that the western members have thought so much on this question that they have failed to realize its significance.
There were other matters, Mr. Speaker, to which I might refer, but I shall not take occasion at this time to put any further figures on Hansard. I have only to say that I cannot vote for the amendment because it declares for free trade, neither can I vote for the budget on account of the reciprocity resolution which it contains. I am therefore under the necessity for voting against both.
Mr. R. J. \\ OODS (Dufferin): Mr. Speaker, in offering a few remarks in connection with the budget I do not propose to charge the government with responsibility for all the ills at present prevailing in the Dominion of Canada in connection with industrial or agricultural or labour conditions. I am confident that it would be impossible for any government to discover a panacea for all those ills, but I am convinced that the government are responsible for the fiscal policy of the country; therefore I feel quite free to offer some criticisms in connection with the present budget.
To my mind the government of the day have had-possibly still have-a dual policy.
I have had more or less to do with political contests on the back concessions and in the rural sections of Ontario for thirty years or

The Budget-Mr. Woods
more, so that I am not entirely a stranger to political contests, to what has been advocated on the hustings, or to the legislation that has been enacted in connection with our fiscal policy As I have viewed it during the last thirty years or more, the political parties have had a double policy, one for the time during which they sat on the opposition benches and the other while they sat on the government side. So that from that point of view in any case I am justified in offering some criticism of the minister's budget for the present year.
The Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart), in his address yesterday, told us that the government were moving in the direction of lower tariff. Well, in watching the history of the Liberal party for a considerable length of time I have been impressed by the fact that the motion has been very slow. According to the statements made, and according to what is put before the people in political campaigns, the party now in power have been moving in that direction for a great number of years. I have tried to view the situation honestly and fairly, but my observation is that the progress has been so slow that it has been almost impossible to detect a movement during the last thirty years so far as reduction of the customs tariff is concerned. So that if the government continues to move as slowly in the future as it has in the past, a lot of us boys who are sitting in the House at the present time will have passed out oi existence so far as this world is concerned before there is any considerable reduction in the customs tariff.
There is one thing I want to commend the government for, and that is the proposal of a reciprocity agreement with the great nation to the south of us. That proposal has been objected to by some hon. members of this House. I think it was the member for East York (Mr. Harris) who suggested yesterday that the people of Canada were not in favour of entering into an agreement with the United States on trade matters, were not in favour of our standing at the door of the United States begging for an opportunity to carry on our trade. So far as my experience and knowledge goes of the rural people at least they are very, very anxious that such an agreement be brought about, for those of us engaged in agriculture know the benefits that we received while we had an open door into the country to the south of us for our natural products. So I want to congratulate the government upon this step and I hope that negotiations will proceed and the agreement be brought about as speedily as possible.
Does not the hon. member admit that this is a step towards lowei tariffs?

I will possibly answer that question before I get through, though perhaps not just as directly as the hon. member would wish, but if he follows me closely I think he will find something that will answer his question.
To prove to this House the benefits that the agriculturists of this country at least received while we had access to that open market in the United States I am going to quote from the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce. During the first ten months under the United States Emergency Tariff Canada's exports to the United States of the principal articles affected by the new duties fell, when compared with the corresponding period of the previous fiscal year, from $157,000,000 to 836,000,000. The principal items included in those totals are wheat and cattle. The value of wheat exports fell from $91,000,000 to $13,500,000, and the quantity from 42,000.000 bushels to 11,000,000 bushels. The value of cattle shipments for the same period fell from $21,000,000 to $3,000,000, or from 280,000 head to 143,000 head. So it is apparent that the agriculturists of this country received a wonderful advantage through that open door. It was a great benefit to them to have that open market, and it is our most natural market being right at our door to which to ship our cattle and other products free.
I want now to refer to the tax on cheques in respect to which legislation was brought down in this budget. Personally I am not favourable to that tax. When the Minister of Finance brought down his budget a year ago his first intimation was that cheques should be taxed two cents for each unit of fifty dollars to the full amount of the cheque, but later the tax was changed to a maximum of $2, so that on a cheque over $5,000 only the maximum of $2 was paid and the unit principle ceased. Personally I was not favourable to a maximum being set. The Finance Minister goes a step further in this budget and reduces the maximum from $2 to $1. In that respect this appears to me to be a rich man's budget. A great deal of the business done in our small towns and cities by small merchants, cattle dealers and so forth is done by cheque, and their cheques are usually small. Now they are compelled to pay two cents on every unit of $50 or less no matter how many cheques they issue, while the man doing a large volume of business and paying out hundreds of thousands of dollars pays
The Budget-Mr. Woods

nothing on a cheque beyond a certain amount. His maximum tax on any cheque, no matter how large, is to be one dollar. I claim that that is very unfair, it works an injustice. I am not going to find fault with the two cent stamp on cheques, not by any means, I think that is a very nice way to raise revenue; but I say that in all fairness to the masses of the people who do business on a small scale and issue many cheques for comparatively small amounts, and who are taxed two cents on every unit of 850, the rich man who issues cheques for large sums of money should be taxed in exactly the same proportion and should pay two cents on every $50 no matter what the size of the cheque issued.
Now, I want to refer for a few moments to the tariff. We have heard occasionally about the high tariff on goods entering the United States. It is true that the United States has a very high tariff, and of course as a justification for keeping up the tariff here hon. gentlemen will sometimes point to the tariff wall on the other side of the line. But while that is true in the general, the United States government has taken cognizance of the needs of the agricultural interests of that country. They have looked well to the interests of the producer. The United States imposes no duty on farm implements of production entering that country, these implements go in there absolutely free. Wagons, threshing machines, cultivators, binders, mowers, reapers, ploughs, harrows, all farm implements enter the United States duty free. But on this side there is a duty of from 10 to 1-7J per cent on wagons, 15 per cent on ploughs, cultivators and so forth, ancT 10 per cent on binders and mowers. It appears to me that if the United States government are so interested in the agriculturists of that country that they can give this advantage to the farmers who cultivate the soil and produce the grain and food that the masses of the people in that country require, the government of this country ought to be as deeply interested in the agriculturists of Canada and give them the same advantage	in their work of	production.
I want to bring to my assistance in this debate, and just in this connection, a speech delivered by the present leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) in the session of 1910-11. I expressed the opinion, when I first began to speak, that there was a dual policy on the part of this government, and it seems to me that in this respect the members of the present administration are not altogether alone; there are possibly some others who are practically in the same boat. If I remember rightly, at 
the time the right hon. gentleman delivered that speech a large deputation of farmers from the West had waited upon the government of that day and had insisted, I believe, practically on free trade in agricultural implements; at any rate, if they did not ask for absolute free trade in this line they demanded a great reduction. I am going to quote now some brief extracts from Hansard in which the right hon. gentleman's speech on that particular occasion is reported. You will find it at page 1915 of Hansard of 1910-11, volume 1. A resolution was introduced by the right hon. gentleman, and I quote it:
That in the opinion of this House a substantial reduction in the import duties on agricultural implements is now due the agriculturists of Canada, and is in just accord with the true ends of the protective tariff.
Of course, I must give my right hon. friend credit for this, that he upheld at that time the same idea of protection. However, let me quote another extract from the same speech; it will be found at page 1917 of the same volume.
They have allowed-
Referring to the government then, in power.
They have allowed, in the respect which I am discussing this afternoon, protection to mn rampant, and they have for reasons that are only too obvious, become the slaves of those who helped them into power and who now maintain them there behind ramparts of gold.
In the face of such a statement as that coming from the right hon. the present leader of the Opposition, I think that the group of gentlemen who surround me here and who all advocate a reduction in the customs tariff in connection with agricultural imnlements, will surely enlist the sympathy and support of the right hon. gentleman. But 1 cannot help remarking that if the government in 1910 were standing behind ramparts of gold they are to-day still standing behind the same fortress; for as we are all aware, while the duty has been reduced, I think, on binders, which at that time paid 174 per cent whereas to-day the duty is 10 per cent, the duty on ploughs is still 15 per cent, with similar rates on harrows and other necessaries of that description. So that there is not such a wonderful difference, after all, in that direction. But we must bear in mind this important fact, that implements in 1910 were slightly over half their present price, and in dollars and cents the protection which is afforded to-day on these implements is greater than it was at that time. The price is well nigh double what it was in 1910; and notwithstanding that there has been a slight reduction in the rate of duty, the actual amount in dollars and cents paid on these

The Budget-Mr. Woods
implements coming from the other side is considerably more than it was in 1910.
Take boots and shoes as another example. If agricultural implements are of great importance to the farmers of Canada, it will not be denied that boots and shoes are an absolute necessity to all of the people throughout the Dominion; and if it is desirable to reduce the duty on agricultural implements, in my opimon the duty on boots and shoes should undoubtedly also be reduced. Boots and shoes to-day are going to the United States free of duty, while we are taxed in this country from 25 to 30 per cent for them.
Fifteen per cent British preference.

I am referring to the general tariff; the duty is 25 to 30 per cent. But the United States admits boots and shoes absolutely free. Yet we are told that if the customs tariff were reduced the manufacturers of the country would suffer. It strikes me that, seeing that labour, according to evidence given before the Agricultural Conditions committee, is practically about the same- this being also very largely true of material- if the manufacturers of the United States can turn out agricultural implements and boots and shoes and throw them upon the world's markets in open competition with all other countries including Canada, the Canadian manufacturers of these same goods should be able to compete in the same markets with the producers to the south of us.
Would the hon. member say to what extent the boot and shoe manufacturers of Canada are exporting shoes to the United States at the present time?

According to the evidence given before the Agricultural Conditions committee a few days ago, if my memory serves me,-and I think I have the facts here -a shoe manufacturer in his testimony practically stated that there were no exports of boots and shoes from Canada to the United States. But let us not forget this, that the boot and shoe manufacturers of Canada hold a monopoly of this industry in this country. When these goods from the United States are debarred by a duty of from 25 to 30 per cent the practical effect is to give the manufacturers in this country an absolute monopoly of the home market.
While they have a larger market in the United States as well.

Yes; they have free access to the United States market, so that if they have any surplus in Canada they can place it there. I am going to bring the House back again to another quotation from the speech by the right hon. leader of the Opposition delivered in, 1910, to be found on page 1,931 of Hansard of that year. He said:
Now, sir, what are the manufacturers of agricultural implements enabled to do? They are able under this tariff to exact a higher price than they could exact if the tariff were lower.
And then a little further on, on page 1933, he said:
They have not only given the manufacturers a grip on the whole home market, but practically, given them a monopoly of it, and they have taxed the consumer in order to push the manufacturers and their industries successfully into the markets of the world.
Now I believe that statement of the right hon. member in 1910 is absolutely true, that the customs tariff of this country and the protection that the manufacturers have had for forty years have given the manufacturers a grip on the home markets of this country, and practically given them a monopoly of those markets and enabled them, as the right hon. gentleman has stated, to push their manufactured goods into the other markets of the world.
But what are the conditions in regard to agriculture? The farmers of this country have not a home market for the produce of the soil. True, there may be a few farmers living in close proximity to our large urban centres who will benefit by being in touch with the markets there because products can be brought to the city markets and sold to the consumers without passing through the hands of a middleman. In that regard the farmeis of this country are benefited, but how many? Very few of the farmers of the Dominion of Canada are in the happy position that they can bring their products to those markets in the urban centres and sell them directly to the consumer, without passing them through the hands of the middlemen. The home markets are practically worthless to the farmers, because we have to put our surplus products on the markets of the world. According to the figures in the report of the Department of Trade and Commerce last year, we exported, in vegetable and animal products, the products of the farm, 8233,892,749 worth more than we imported. In the animal and vegetable products of the farm this country has exported goods to that amount more than have been imported of the same quality of goods. The producers of these goods have
The Budget-Mr. Woods

no home market, speaking on broad lines for goods have to go to the open markets of the world. This boasted home market that the tariff has built up-and we have had many, public addresses along that line-has been built up for the manufacturers Then again we are referred to the revenue, and the fact is pointed out that we need a customs tariff for revenue. We know that considerable revenue is derived from the customs tariff, but it is quite possible that a lower tariff might bring equally as much revenue or possibly more. We see an example of that in the statement made by the Einance Minister (Mr. Fielding) in regard to cigarettes in his budget speech. The duty on cigarettes was practically a prohibitive duty and the reduction of that duty was made in the hope that it might bring in more revenue. What is true in [DOT] regard to that is certainly true in regard to other commodities. To my mind a revenue tariff works in the reverse way, because of the fact that it is too high, and we might possibly receive more revenue with a lower tariff, and it would impose less burden on the consuming public.
Now again I am going to refer to the speech of the right hon. member (Mr. Meighen) delivered in 1910, to verify the statement which I have made. At page 1,933 of the same Hansard he said:
I say that to my mind this tariff is designed to benefit the revenues of other countries rather than the revenues of our own countries. As at present constituted this is not so much a tariff for the revenue of Canada as a tariff for the revenue of Spain, as a tariff for the revenue of Austria. ... It is, Sir, a tariff for the revenue of Roumania, a tariff for the revenue of Russia, a tariff for the revenue of France rather than a tariff for the revenue of Canada.
That quotation verifies the statement I have just made in regard to the high tariff being to some extent prohibitive, and that a marked reduction in that tariff might be the means of bringing more revenue to this country than it does at the present time.
I wish to refer now to the tariff as being a means of centralizing the industries of the Dominion of Canada. I think the hon. member for North Waterloo, (Mr. Euler) in his speech some time ago, advised our friends from the West-if my memory serves me right, and I think it does-to start manufacturing industries all over the West.
Hear, hear.

It would be a wonderful thing to start manufacturing industries all over the West and build up a home market. It has been proven conclusively, to my mind at least, that with our present population, and 
until it reaches to millions and millions more than we have at the present time, we have practically no home market for the agricultural products of this country.
I was also in favour of the policy of immigration-to let the peocile come in.

I also hope we will get immigration. What has this done for the small manufacturer? I refer chiefly to Ontario, because I am not so much acquainted with the other provinces of the Dominion, so far as industries are concerned, but I have known something about the conditions in the province of Ontario for the last forty or fifty years. I am sure that I am correct when I state that 30 or 40 years ago scattered throughout Ontario in almost every little village there were one or two manufacturing establishments which supplied the great bulk of the needs of the people in those commodities. They were small foundries where men got their ploughs, their cultivators, their farm implements to a great extent, outside possibly of binders. They got their mowers. Personally I might state that the first mower we ever got on our farm I bought for $40 from a home manufacturer right at my own door. I cut wood in the bush and paid for it. We never had a more substantial mowing machine on our farm from that day to this, and we have had quite a number of them. That, however, is a thing of the past, because those small industries have been either swamped or bought out, I do not know which. There is no question that they have disappeared. We are at a loss, to a large extent, even in getting our repairs which we formerly got from those little manufacturing establishments that we had in our communities. They built our threshing machines, our horse-power machines, many of our farm implements, such as ploughs and so forth. Those establishments have now disappeared. In those days we could take our grist to the mill, have our wheat ground and our flour returned to us along with the by-products, bran and shorts. Those mills have all disappeared. We could take our oats to the mill and get our oatmeal back with us. Those mills too have all disappeared. The reason is that the manufacturers of this country have been so protected that they have built up gigantic industries in the great urban centres, and from the rural communities they have drawn the labourers, the farmers, many of our people who should be on the farms to-day, operating and cultivating the soil. Those people have been drawD

The Budget-Mr. Woods
off to the great urban centres because of the centralization of the manufacturing industries of this country. I believe the protective tariff has a great deal to do with that condition in Ontario to-day.
But then we are told that where they have a greater volume of business, where they have larger machines, they can manufacture the implements so much more cheaply in those great factories than could be done in the small factories. I believe that is true; but who reaps the benefit of those cheap manufactured goods? Who are the beneficiaries? It is not the farmers back on the farm, but the manufacturers that receive the benefit by manufacturing more cheaply and at the same time holding up the price of their goods under the protective policy of this country. I am going to give an illustration of that. In the constituency which I have the honour to represent there is one small factory that has weathered the storm. It has not weathered the storm as regards manufacturing new implements to any extent; but it still carries on by manufacturing repairs for the implements in that community. I am going to give to the House figures that are absolutely correct. In 1921, that foundry in the constituency that I represent was selling ploughshares to the farmers at 50 cents apiece. It was sending them out over the community wherever people would send in an order for them, and while of course, there would be the freight, that would be a very small trifle for a ploughshare going a short distance by railway over the constituency. I asked that manufacturer what he was selling these ploughshares for, and he said: "I am selling them for 50 cents apiece and I am sending them out by the hundreds." At the very time that that small manufacturer was selling ploughshares at 50 cents apiece, our local dealers, who were agents for the large manufacturing companies of this country, were charging us from 90 cents to SI .20 for the same ploughshares. Who was receiving the benefit? If the small manufacturer could make ploughshares at 50 cents apiece, why could the manufacturers not make those ploughshares, send them out and sell them through their local agents for 65 or 70 cents apiece? It is the large manufacturers who have received the benefit of cheaper manufacture in the great centres, and this, I claim, is due to centralization largely brought about through the protection that is given to the manufacturers by the customs tariff.
I am going to refer to another matter that has been thrown in our face occasionally,
and that is that when the Reciprocity agreement .vas before the people of the Dominion of Canada, the farmers turned it down. In my opinion, to a large extent we are guilty; but so far as my knowledge goes in connection with that particular campaign as it was carried on in the locality in which I live-and I think that would be a fair sample of what went en i * the various localities in Ontario

I did not know of any Liberals in the past who were farmers turning against the Liberal party and going over and voting with the Conservatives. I knew of no Liberals who forsook the Liberal party because of the Reciprocity agreement.
Not real ones.

So in regard to that, the
farmers are not really guilty. If the farmers had turned over from the Conservative ranks and voted Liberal in strong numbers, we might have succeeded, and I am sorry that they did not. So far as I
5 p.m. know they did not do so to any great extent in the rural sections. What was the result in the urban centres? What was the attitude of the Liberals in the great urban centres, the industrial Liberals of the Dominion of Canada, in connection with the Reciprocity agreement?

The noble eighteen of
Toronto.

That was just what I was
going to refer to. Eighteen Liberals signed a manifesto to oppose that Reciprocity agreement, and if my memory serves me aright. I think amongst that number was Sir Thomas White who was honoured with the position of Minister of Finance of the Dominion of Canada.
By the Tories.

But he turned over from
Liberalism.
Yes.

That is to my mind conclusive evidence that the manufacturers of this country are behind the government that will protect them. They are behind the government for class legislation. Although the Progressive group has been charged with coming into existence to seek class legislation for the farmers, this group came into existence because we had to fight class legislation in the Dominion of Canada. Many of us would have been tilling our land to-day if it had not been for the very fact that the farmers of this country had been burdened through class legislation in the interest of the manufactur-
The Budffet-Mr. Euler

mg industries. That is the reason why tlr group is here to-day. We are on the job, we are going to stay on the job, and we are going to fight for equal rights to all and special privileges to none.
Will my hon. friend aid us in starting that campaign by moving the permanent suspension of the Crowsnest rates?

We will see how things are going to work out in the future. So far as my observation goes, our tariff legislation for the last thirty or forty years is the joint product of the Liberal and Conservative parties, and both parties are in the one boat as respects fiscal policy. In a word, which ever party happened to be in power never failed to receive support of the manufacturing interests, because quite naturally these interests always stand behind the party that stands for protection in this Dominion.

Mr. Speaker, before entering upon the observations which I intend to make on the budget proper, I should like to join in the congratulations which have been tendered by other members to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) on the presentation of his seventeenth budget. And I do this for two reasons; first, because he has established a record that is unique in the management of the Finance department of Canada and, secondly, because he is held to-day, after twenty-five years of office beginning in 1896, in just as great regard by the people of Canada as ever. I further congratulate him because of the budget which he has brought down at this time. I do not suppose that my hon. friends opposite will agree with me, but I think the Minister of Finance has presented a budget which ought to meet with the general approval of the people of Canada. I do not suppose that he himself would claim that his budget is entirely perfect. It may be capable of improvement. Indeed, there may be one or two features of it with which I would not agree myself. But in a country such as we have, with its diversified interests,
I realize, and I think all members should realize, that it is necessary to grant something to the spirit of compromise.
True, the budget has met with some criticism, but this criticism has not been very strong. I should like to approach the consideration of the budget in a broad way and from a national viewpoint. It has sometimes been said that Canada is a very difficult country to govern. I believe that to be true. We know the Maritime provinces came into 
confederation unwillingly; they felt they were losing their natural market in the United States, and for it they claimed they were not compensated by the market which they hoped to get in central Canada, in the provinces of Ontario and Quebec; and to-day many of their people find it difficult to make ends meet because of that disadvantage. Farther west we have the industrial provinces of Quebec and Ontario where, rightly or wrongly, the people feel that a moderate tariff is necessary for the preservation of their industries. Going still farther west we have the prairie provinces where again, rightly or wrongly, the people feel that no tariff at all or a very, very moderate tariff indeed is in their interests. And then across the Rocky mountains we have a mixed population whose ideas vary on the subject of the tariff. All of which, Mr. Speaker, merely goes to prove that if we are to have national unity we must each of us, though our interests vary, yield something for the common good. And that is why I support the budget.

I would write off the difference between the actual value so ascertained and the amount of indebtedness which is now charged against the railroads, upon a large portion of which we require to pay fixed charges, although those fixed charges are based on fictitious assets. I take that position because the money was lost, we have

nothing to show for it, and we might as well write it off and not have the fictitious assets as a perpetual handicap upon the road. This action would not reduce our losses in actuality, of course; but it would reduce the enormous aggregate of fixed charges which the roads are expected to earn, and which figure so largely in the annual deficit. If this were done it would be an encouragement to the board of directors. Not only would it encourage the management who would not be continually confronted with the task of trying to make earnings on an over-capitalization, but it would put the National Railways on more of an equality with their great competitor, the Canadian Pacific Railway. I believe also if that were done, it would be only a short time until our National Railways would be on a sound financial basis. The profit and loss account would soon show a balance on the credit side, which could then be applied to a reduction of rates which is so much desired.
Some weeks ago the leader of the Opposition (Mr. Meighen) suggested that these losses and fictitious assets, as I have called them, should be carried along with the idea that, in future years as the roads became more prosperous, we would be able to draw dividends, if we want to call them such, on these amounts. I am not disposed to agree with that, because I do not believe it would be businesslike to carry on the books, assets which are not real assets. If after a time we find that the rates do show profits over and above operating costs and fixed charges, under the plan that I propose, it becomes merely a matter of policy whether these profits shall be applied to wipe out the old losses t>r whether they should be applied to a reduction of rates. Frankly, I think they should be applied to a reduction of rates because the real theory and purpose of public ownership is not the making of profits, but the giving of the best possible service at cost.

Mr. Speaker, in rising to discuss the budget I wish to extend my hearty congratulations to the hon. Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding), who on this occasion is delivering his seventeenth budget. He has rendered very valuable and faithful services to this country, services extending over very many years, and I can pay him no greater compliment than to say that to-day he possesses the esteem of the people from one end of Canada to the other.
It has been pleasing to us in this quarter of the House to note that our friends who now occupy the government benches are at last coming round to the view that we must have a certain amount of protection and that under present conditions, with other countries raisina high tariff walls, it would be unfair to Canada to cut down our tariff, particularly when i' would be so hard to obtain revenue from other sources to make up for any loss caused by a revision downwards.
We have to take into consideration, too, the competition that our manufacturers would have to meet in the event of our lowering the tariff on certain articles that we now manufacture. We have not only competition from the United States, where they manufacture in such large volume that they are able to,put their goods on the market at a cheaper rate than we can compete with, but we have another source of competition that has not had much attention paid to it in past years, although I think now we are beginning to wake up to the danger. I refer to competition from the hundreds of millions of people on the other side of the Pacific with cheap water transportation to our shores. We find Japan is branching out in many lines of manufacture, and in a very short time, in fact even to-day, with her splendid steamship service across the Pacific she is able to place her "merchandise on our markets at lower prices in some cases than we can quote ourselves.
I am very pleased indeed to note that the government proposes to give a bonus for the manufacture of certain lines of copper. This will beneficially affect one of the big smelters in British Columbia. I know that smelter very well. This little town would go out of existence were it not for the Trail smelter. As we look over the agricultural situation in Canada and throughout the world we find that the markets on which we have been depending for a number of years and on which our agriculture was very largely built up, are very much disorganized. Some of them are entirely out of existence; others are much more limited than they were before. This condition, of course, has a serious effect upon agriculture in this country. Some of our farmers are meeting with reverses in regard to the disposal of their product; owing to climatic conditions, bad crops and so forth some of them are losing heart and, I think, leaving the country. But this is not the first depression we have had in Canada; we have had even worse depressions than this in former years and we have lived through them all. I feel quite satisfied that with the spirit of the Canadian people behind us we will survive the present one.
We must not, however, criticize the farmer too severely. In fact, no one is in a position to criticize the farmer unless he has himself experienced some of the ups and downs of agriculture. Those of us who were brought up in the country, particularly in the wooded
The Budget-Mr. Tohnie

sections, know what it is to rough it on the farm, to go out and do half a day's work on a plate of porridge-and I may say in that connection that my father came from Inverness, Scotland. At the same time I do not feel that we are going to get anywhere by blindly complaining of our condition. It appears to me that the most practical thing to do under the circumstances is to make a careful survey of the situation and then to select those lines of agriculture that will give to us the quickest and best promise of success. In doing this I think at the very beginning we can score rather severely that particular line of farming known as single crop farming. In fact, where it depends on the production of one line of grain in some sections of the country, it develops into very little more than a gamble with the weather. But the man who gambles on the single crop is rather at a disadvantage compared with the man who gambles in other lines, because he is limited to only one bet a year. If he wins that bet he probably winters in California; if he does not win it he stays at home and tells us that the country is no good. Now, it is admitted-and judging from the debate that has taken place already it is generally accepted in this country -that our most reliable line of agriculture is that of mixed farming with live stock as a basis. This is the safer plan even for the man who wishes to specialize in a particular line; if he at least keeps a certain amount of live stock for a nucleus he can radiate from this centre as far as he likes, and the chances are, if the live stock markets are in any sort of reasonable condition, that the results of his work in that direction will carry him through many of the hard places in connection with the single crop on which he has concentrated much of his attention.
There never was a time in Canada when it was so necessary to carry on a system of good farming as it is to-day. When prices are high we may practise hit and miss farming to a certain extent and meet with fair success, but under conditions like those which prevail at present, with prices low and costs high, it is necessary to apply the very best methods if we are to succeed.
There is another thing that is very important, too, and that is the plugging up of the leaks to the best of our ability. Produce all we can at home, make the farms selfsustaining, and at the same time send nothing to market but what is of the best quality possible, in the best condition, and marketed at the proper time. In that way we can make a very substantial saving. Let us glance for

a moment at the situation with regard to marketing and the quality and condition of the stock sold in the markets of this country, and then form an opinion whether the farmer is at the present time making the best of his opportunities. Last year we sold 600,000 head of cattle through our inspected abattoirs, and it is estimated that owing to poor quality, poor condition and small size the farmers of this country dropped $30,000,000. A comparison of the prices will be rather interesting. Another branch of the live stock industry and one of the most reliable, I think, is that of dairying. Dairying is one of our most stable industries; even to-day, in those cases where cheapness of production is well taken care of and good breeding has been attended to so that the herds contain animals of fairly high quality, a very reasonable profit is returned to the farmer. But again the result depends very largely on the farmer himself. I will show you that we are losing every year an amount estimated at 1200,000,000 owing to the poor quality of the dairy cows in Canada. We have 3,500,000 dairy cows in this country that average about 3,500 pounds of milk each per year, while we have single cows in Canada that yield as high as 33,000 pounds in a year, or a little over eight times as much as the average yield. The farmer who maintains scrub cows has to keep a stable that will hold eight cows instead of one. He has to feed eight cows, clean out the places for eight cows, milk eight cows, and after he gets through with it all there is very little profit in it for him. The man who maintains a better herd- and some of our herds average as high as 14,000 pounds of milk per cow for the whole herd-does not talk about hard times, while the man who maintains a scrub herd is always doing so.
One of the greatest jokes in connection with the agricultural business, if there are any such-my experience is that it is always pretty hard work-is to hear a man complain about the failure to take the duty off agricultural implements while at the same time he is trying to make a living out of a 4,000 pound cow. It is an utter impossibility. If he would just take care of his herd, get the proper kind of cows and breed them up, improve their quality, I do not think the duty at present existing on agricultural implements would interfere with him very much. It has been found at some of our experiment stations that as the yield of the cow increases, the cost of production goes down up to a point, of 18,076 pounds per year, and in thole cases where the milk was of a fairly high quality the cost still kept lowering. But where the butter fat content is rather low we find that above that figure the cost of production is a little higher, but at the same time still quite profitable.
While the improvement of herds may be looked upon by some as something that cao only be accomplished by a rich man, I may say that at the Nappan experiment station down in the Maritime provinces an experiment was conducted of taking a number of scrub cows from neighbouring farmers and placing them on the farm, and just by good feeding alone the product was increased by fifty per cent Then by proper breeding methods the output of the offspring of these cows was increased fifty per cent again, showing that there is a proposition within easy reach of any farmer, and one where good results can be accomplished by a combination of proper breeding and feeding. The farmer who stili maintains a scrub herd and has not yet tried to improve its condition should not be downhearted. I know of my own personal knowledge many cases where farmers have commenced with scrub cows and after a few years have been able to reach over 12,000, 13,000 and 14,000 pounds of milk per cow, and in addition to that 550 pounds of butter fat per cow, showing that this is within easy reach of any farmer who has the energy and perseverance to try. Of course, this was not done by making speeches. It was done by being willing to work, to learn and improve. These men I particularly speak of took every possible opportunity to improve themselves, improve their knowledge of dairying by visiting experiment stations, exhibitions and the best herds in the country, and I am quite sure that anyone who will display the same intelligence and energy as they did will have very satisfactory results.
Our dairy industry last year was wortu about $240,000,000 to this country. Our export market is that of Great Britain. We send some dairy products to the United States, but Great Britain, I think, is the more important market of the two. We have been having rather bad results over there during the last year or two owing to the fact that, our butter is not coming up to the demands of the British market. As you may know, in that market we have to meet very strong competition from Denmark, Holland and also New Zealand. The Britisher complains that our butter is too heavily salted. Some people say that the salt is put in to meet the taste of the people in Canada, while others ex plain that salt sells for two cents a pound and butter for forty or fifty cents a pound. The Britisher also complains that our butter is uneven in colour, that its flavouring is not first-class, and that it is also defective in keeping qualities. To illustrate that I may say that our butter sells in Great Britain from
