Let us glance for a moment at the hog and export bacon industry. Perhaps no line of live stock has suffered so much from in-and-out farming, that is to say, the farmer has gone into the hog business when prices were high and dropped out of it when prices were low, and very often by that system he has missed the high prices and failed to get the advantages the other man has secured who has stayed steadily in the business. At the Central experimental farm at Ottawa it has been clearly demonstrated that on land valued at $125 an acre, where regular wages were paid, where they did not have the benefit of family help, hogs paid every year during the war and since that time. But during that very period there were men out in certain sections of Canada where grain was a little cheaper than here who were going out of the hog business because they said hogs did not pay.
Let us see whether the farmer has made the most of his opportunities in connection with the hog industry. Our markets to-day are

suffering very severely owing to the fact that the farmer fails to send to those markets hogs of the proper type and proper weight. This not only injures the farmer himself but the packer also. It very seriously interferes with his work, and particularly in his effort to secure a fair share of the British market. There are eight packing plants doing business in Ontario, and at these plants forty-five per cent of the hogs marketed are what are known as out-weights. The ideal weight for a hog to furnish a Wiltshire side for the British market will run from 160 to 210 pounds live weight. These hogs that are not of the right type seriously interfere with the sale of our goods on the other side of the water. To illustrate, let me say that recently at a sale of Canadian Wiltshire sides held in England the desirable weights brought from 101s. to 102s. per hundredweight of 112 pounds, while out-weights that did not conform with the requirements brought only 94s. And still the farmer continues to market these out-weights even in face of the fact that there is a difference of one or two cents a pound on the live hogs as they are taken into the abattoir.
There were 2,000,000 hogs slaughtered in our plants in the year 1922. Of these, 40 per cent, or 800,000 were required for export; and in the grading of these 800,000, only 13 per cent were classed as selected bacon type. If all the selects had been exported they would have supplied only about 32-5 per cent of the packers' requirements, with the result that the packer is now compelled to buy many of the out-weights and fat types to meet the market demands. What effect has this on him? This is simply one of the reasons why Danish bacon, with the uniform supply from that country, will sell in the British market at 117 shillings per hundredweight, while the best Canadian bacon sells at between 102 and 105 shillings and on the average only 96 shillings per hundredweight. It hag been clearly shown that our best hogs are equal in every way to the Danish product, and the cure given by our packers in this country is altogether on a par with that given to the product of the European packing houses. By way of illustration I might quote the following from a letter received from a gentleman a short time ago who spent some time in England. He says:
One day last week I tested Canadian bacon against Irish and Danish, without knowing the position of the three. By long odds everyone was in favour of one kind, which turned out to be Canadian; and yet we have to take many shillings a hundred-weight less for our product.
What is the reason for this? The explanation is simply that, as I have pointed out,

The Budget-Mr. Tolmie
our supply is uneven both in quality and in weight. There appears to be no excuse for our not being able to produce a good quality in Canada. We have a great variety of grains which I think are equal for these purposes to any grown in the world. In the United States they produce their hogs largely on a corn diet, with the result as shown in the figures which I will give to the House bearing on the question, comparing the prices received for American Wiltshire sides as against Canadian Wiltshires. The American Wiltshires brought 90 shillings per hundredweight, while the best Canadian product sold at 105 shillings; and the average American product brought 80 shillings as against the average Canadian 96 shillings. The American, in addition to feeding his hogs on com, raises what is known as the thick fat hog, which goes largely to lard. This is a type that the Englishman is not very fond of. He got a surfeit of it during the war and I am afraid it will take some time before he recovers from his experience with American pork.
A comparison of the prices at Chicago with those obtaining in Toronto during the year ending March 31,	1923, shows that the
smallest difference beween the Chicago and the Toronto price was in favour of the Toronto price to the extent of $1.45. That was during the month of October. The higher price in favour of Toronto in the month of July was $3.97 wThile the average for the twelve months was $3.16, showing that the Canadian farmer marketing his product in Toronto and the other markets that contribute thereto, obtains a higher price than if he had his hogs in Chicago when hogs are sold there. This is largely due to the demand for his particular type of hog, as I have shown; and with the feed at the disposal of the Canadian breeder and feeder, he is able to send pork to market in a firmer condition than can the man who has to depend entirely on corn.
Let me say however that while we are competing in the British market with the Dane, while we produce our own feeds at home, the Dane has to depend to a great extent on feeds exported from other countries. In view of this fact, surely we should be able to compete with him if we pay particular attention to the article we send abroad and see to it that it is uniform and of the kind demanded. While the type of hog produced in Canada, the price of which is controlled by the export market, fetches the prices I have quoted, there is to be taken into consideration this fact that the producers of hogs in Canada enjoy a certain form of protection. According to our health of animals regulations it is illegal to import hogs from the United States for slaughtering purposes, or indeed, for that matter, for any purpose at all, unless they are quarantined for thirty days at the boundary line. With such a regulation in force, it would not pay anyone to import hogs, unless for breeding purposes and of high value, and incur the expenses connected with this quarantine. This therefore is a form of protection. It was not intended as such, but in fact it is protection and that is one reason for the price the Canadian producer enjoys in the home market.
Another interesting point I might mention. We might compare the prices of grain grown in this country and used for hog feed, such as barley, eorn, bran and shorts, with the hog prices received during the war. Last year we find the. ratio between the prices of feed and of hogs more favourable than in 1914 or at any time during the war, which shows that the opportunities of the producer of pork at the present time are better than they have been for ten years. However, careful feeding is absolutely necessary. Recently out of a shipment of some 2,500 head of hogs sent to one of our abattoirs, 400 carcases were classed as "softs" owing to improper feeding. There is a great scarcity of hogs of the proper type of weight and finish. To obtain these hogs more attention must be paid to breeding and feeding operations. The market will increase and our product will equal the Danish product if we send the kind of material which is called for in London and at other points in Great Britain where our products are used. We need to exercise great care in the selection of breeding stock with a view to securing the proper type. We must also market our product at the right time. One of the failings of the Canadian breeder is that he sends mixed lots of hogs to the market, some of which conform with the requirements, securing the highest prices, others being too heavy, having been kept too long, and others, again, too light, not having been fed long enough. This is another instance in which the farmer must help himself. Neither the government nor anyone else can help him in this regard if he does not take the initiative. With regard to this Canadian market, I have no doubt of the possibility of our being able to secure our full share. There is no question about that. The conditions are favourable, but if the farmers show indifference

with regard to the type of hog they produce, we may easily find ourselves among the tail-enders in the British market.
There is another line of live stock which I think should be doing very much better than it has done in the past in Canada. It is one in regard to which we are very much behind other agricultural countries, not only of the British Empire but in the world at large. I refer to the production of sheep and wool. The number of sheep in Canada to-day does not exceed three or three and a quarter million head as compared with twenty seven millions in Great Britain, forty millions in the United States and eighty millions in Australia. This has been due largely to the fact that while the market in Canada has been of an unstable nature, prices varying up and down, there has been no encouragement for men to go into this business. This particular industry, I think, should receive every assistance possible. We have been allowing Great Britain to ship her wool over to Italy and Germany, where it is combed and returned and then shipped into Canada free of duty. This product is known as "tops." We find also that the Japanese are now going into the wool combing business quite extensively, and their goods are coming here free and competing with ours, which is a very unfair competition indeed. I am informed however that there has been in existence for some time a tariff of 15 per cent on combed tops coming into Canada. This 15 per cent has never been enforced and I would urge upon the minister that it be put into effect at the earliest possible date so that our wool combers in this country may secure the protection that they require to build up their industry.
I would even go further than that and give bonuses for the handling of wool in this country until we get the industry on a proper footing. There is something certainly very seriously wrong with an industry when in a huge country like Canada, with vast areas of land, suitable for the raising of sheep, our sheep population amounts to only about three and a half million, particularly in view of the fact, as I pointed out, that you cannot blame it on protection, as far as combed wool is concerned. I would like to draw this matter to the attention of the Minister of Customs (Mr. Bureau) whom I had not noticed in his seat until this moment. I said that we were bringing wool combings into this country absolutely free at the present time, in spite of the fact that we have a tariff of 15 per cent against that class of goods, which has never [Mr. Tolmie.1
been enforced, and I am pressing on the House the necessity of enforcing that tariff at the earliest possible date so as to assist in placing our sheep industry on a proper and substantial footing. It is quite possible for us to produce the highest quality of wool in Canada, capable of manufacturing up to 64s. quality. From that up to 70s. and 80s. we have to import our wool, but it is possible for us to produce the higher grades necessary for the manufacture of that particular quality. We also have competition from Australia, which is sending combed wrool in here without any duty, while in that country the government bonuses wool combing to the extent of 5 or 6 cents per pound. Here the Canadian producer of sheep and the Canadian wool comber have to face during part of the summer, the competition of the bonused wool trade of the greatest sheep-growing country in the world. In addition to that the Australian wool comber is able to buy wool from the hide wool stock accumulated by the Australian government during the war, at cost price and this is another disadvantage which the Canadian wool comber has to contend with. There has also been a reduction in woollen cloth from Great Britain, and in this connection I may say that we should I think be able to build up a few of t these important industries the building up of which means assistance and help to our natural products, such as wool, and many other articles. Let us get our home manufacture of woollen goods at least securely on its feet, and let the wool market become a reliable one, and you will find the sheep population of Canada increasing in very great numbers. The sheep is a useful animal, useful on almost every farm, and one that will live largely on waste material in the summer months. It is a very good animal for keeping down weeds and it furnishes a supply of manure at almost any time of the year. Here is the farmer making the best of his opportunities in the production of lambs. The lamb is a side line of the sheep industry which is very important and one that is very remunerative where carried on in the proper way. We find in Canada that the farmer markets about 70 per cent of his male lamb flocks with the result that there is a great loss in the summer on that particular account. To give you an idea of the size of this market, in the first three months of the year over 28,000 ewes and lambs were marketed in the Toronto market. The lamb market has changed to a great extent. Within recent years lamb feeding has been taken up and the lambs are fed

The Budget-Mr. Tolmie
on the waste material of the wheat grower, known as screenings; and fed properly on that material. Large feeding plants have been established at Calgary, Fort William and other points. With the supply of winter lamb from the feeding plants, it has not been so necessary for the farmer to fill the cold storage plant during the fall of the year. He finds the fresh killed lamb during the winter months will not pay, and that the nursing lamb will not sell so well in the winter when there is fresh lamb to be obtained. I have been listening very attentively to the hon. member and before he leaves the live stock end of it I would like him to go into a little more detail in regard to one point. He stated that the farmers lost some $30,000,000 last year through not keeping the proper class of stock. I would like to know how he arrived at that figure?

It is estimated that the number of animals that went through our packing houses was 600.000 odd. It is based on a calculation made by some of the experts in the Department of Agriculture during the time I was minister in 1919. In 1919 and 1920 there had been exported through our inspected slaughter houses 1,126.000 head of cattle, and less than 10 per cent of these cattle were either good enough in condition or good enough in quality or heavy enough in weight to be exported to Great Britain to compete with the products of other countries. At that time the loss was estimated at some $40,000,000, and this is based on the same figures. I cannot give details, but it was all worked out in proportion. I pointed out that success depends very much on individual effort, that the farmer must be more selfdependent, that while the government can assist him in a general way he must help himself and be ready to co-operate. There is one line however, among others in which the government can render very valuable services
in my opinion, and that is the field of research, particularly in connection with our animal contagious diseases, those that are classed as contagious diseases under our act, and also those that are not classed or scheduled in the Animal Contagious Diseases Act. The two diseases which cause the most loss are tuberculosis and hog cholera. I pointed out some time ago a very marked increase in our inspected abattoirs in tuberculosis, both in cattle and in hogs, having reached the point of nearly 22 per cent on the inspected carcases, those carcases going through our inspected abattoirs where exact returns are kept.
Another disease causing tremendous loss in cattle is infective abortion, a disease affecting horses, sheep and swine. Then there is another disease called the "joint ill," in the foal, one of the most destructive diseases which affects animals. When they become infected with this disease, they die in a very short time.
There is another field for research and that is in regard to internal parasites, which according to the estimates in the United States, has cost that country hundreds of millions per year. In 1921-22 we paid in compensation for tuberculosis $639,530 and in 192223 the sum reached nearly $1,000,000. This does not include the losses on the abattoirs and also'on the farms from affected carcases, which losses would run into many more millions, in my opinion. In the face of this, we are spending only $30,000 a year on research work, and much of this expenditure is required for the manufacture of tuberculin and other such agents for the diagnosing of disease. It is quite possible for an animal to be quite healthy in appearance on the outside, and there is no physical way in which to make a diagnosis so as to decide effectively whether it is affected with tuberculosis or not. We use tuberculin which is applied in three ways:	To the eye, or into
the pores of the skin, or under the skin. By that means and by taking temperatures, watching swellings and so on, we are able to diagnose very effectively whether an animal is affected with tuberculosis or not. We have one serious obstacle in the way, and that is that we cannot separate an animal that is Dadly affected and that would be a spreader of disease amongst other live stock, from an animal that is only slightly affected and that probably, under ordinary conditions, will make a recovery. This is the point. At present we are compelled, when we get that reaction in our tests, to destroy all those animals. If we could discover in our research work a
The Budget-Mr. Tolmie

reagent that would differentiate between an animal that was slightly affected and one that was badly affected, we would make a very substantial saving to the country.
Another feature that offers us great promise is in immunization from tuberculosis. Certain experiments along those lines have been carried on which have given very fair promise, and by proper research work we should be able to discover some serum or bacillus or other biological product which would give us great assistance in that direction. My claim is this, that it does not seem practical to be paying out hundreds of thousands of dollars for compensation without spending much money on research work. We should follow out this research work to the very end of the road and spend any reasonable amount. I can well understand that the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) has a great deal of difficulty in securing sufficient money to carry on his work, and I speak feelingly o:t this subject, because I have been in that position myself. The country, however, will gradually improve and get on its feet, and as opportunity offers, this is a particular branch of our live stock work that should be carried out to the fullest possible extent so far as money will permit.
Another point in connection with research in the direction of bovine tuberculosis is the tremendous field of human tuberculosis which is closely allied to it. It is now generally accepted everywhere that the bovine bacillus is communicable to man, and the discovery of an immunizator, or a discovery in some other direction that would help to overcome this scourge in cattle, would prove of tremendous value to man. We are very fortunate in Canada in having in Doctor Watson, Chief Bacteriologist of the Health of Animals branch, a man of exceptional ability. As an illustration of that, let me point out that only a few years ago in southwestern Saskatchewan and Alberta, we had amongst horses a disease know as glanders. Dr. Watson was placed in charge of the outbreak there; a quarantine station was established at Lethbridge, Alberta, and he was able, while there carrying on his experiments, to discover a blood test by which he could diagnose the disease before any clinical symptoms were shown. When he discovered this test, the amount of compensation paid that year for horses destroyed amounted to $46,000, and I think not more than five or six years had elapsed when the compensation amounted to $75. The next year it was wiped out altogether in Canada. They have been carrying on some experimental work at the Pathological station in Hull in connection with the pro-
duction of a protective or immunizing serum against glanders. While the experiments -were being carried on, a fanner in Manitoba became infected with glanders from a glandered horse. Fortunately a doctor from that province was visiting Ottawa and heard about the immunizing serum discovered by Doctor Watson. He secured some of it, and by the time the serum reached Manitoba, the doctor attending the farmer was also infected with the disease. I know of no other case on record-some hon. members who are doctors will correct me if I am wrong-where glanders in the human body has ever been cured. By the use of this serum, however, I am informed, both the doctor and the farmer are now attending to their business in the usual way, and only a few weeks have elapsed. What I claim is this, that we should cultivate and encourage in every possible way a man of such exceptional ability along the line of research and an appropriation of only $50,000 to be given him would be quite sufficient and could be added to from time to time as the work developed. In that particular connection, it would be advisable under those conditions to have Doctor Watson devote the whole of his time to this special work.
Another line of the greatest importance and, perhaps, the greatest obstacle to the success of the agriculturist in this country is that of distribution, Giving largely to our tremendous distances in Canada and also to the high cost of transportation. It is pretty difficult to find a solution for the problem of what wa should aim to secure in that particular line; but a little investigation will bring us relief, and that is to secure cheaper trans-
9 p.m. portation for the farmer, an equalization of freight rates, and then to allow trade to flow in its natural channels regardless of our big cities trying to draw trade in their direction.
I might draw the attention of the House to the development of trade on the Pacific coast where I am fortunate enough to live. The trade from the Pacific coast across to the Atlantic is now something over a billion or two billion dollars a year. The Panama canal has certainly made a great difference as regards transportation from western to eastern Canada. We should take advantage of all those things because it is most important that the primary producer, the farmer, should secure as large a proportion of the profit from his output as he possibly can. In this par tieular connection, agriculture is of such great importance to the Dominion of Canada that if we could place this industry squarely on its feet and make it profitable to the farmet.

In the development of our markets, a great deal can be done. According to statistics, we market about 80 per cent of our goods at home, either for consumption or for remanufacture for export. Our principal export markets are those of the United States and Great Britain. The United States, as we all know, is quite close to our border; it is easy to reach at low cost; but it has the disadvantage of having a very high tariff. Somehow or another there are 110,000,000 people on the other side of the line who believe in protection, with the result that we find our goods going into that country are very much handicapped by a heavy tariff. Great Britain then is the market that is the most desirable one, although situated at some further distance from our shores. Still it is willing to pay excellent prices and it is one which should be cultivated with the greatest possible attention. During my visit to Great Britain in 1921, I went through a number of the markets. There I found the Britisher anxious to buy our goods, provided they were of good quality, uniform and of sufficient volume to interest him. He was quite willing to pay us just as much as he had to pay to anybody else, but absolutely no more, and you cannot blame him for taking that stand. Another great field is being opened up for us across the Pacific where hundreds of millions of people desire our goods, and this market should be developed to the greatest possible extent.
Another feature that might receive encouragement is that of co-operative selling amongst farmers. Co-operation would enable the farmer to get his goods to market in much better condition, and by being able to load in carload lots, he would secure lower freight rates and be able to market to better advantage.
Long time-credits might also receive attention. In fact this means of helping the farmer is receiving considerable attention now, from what I have heard in the Banking committee and in the committee investigating agricultural conditions. The ordinary banker, while quite satisfactory for the farmer who is on his feet, cannot be expected to make longterm loans. That is not his business. Some other organization must be developed for this particular purpose of making long term loans at the lowest possible rate. However, there is one thing to be pointed out in this connection, and that is that the farmer who has been unable to make ends meet owing to being on a poor farm or following bad method' cannot look for very much help from borrowed
money, whether he obtains it at a low or a high rate of interest. To succeed he must either change on to another farm or adopt proper farming methods.
There is another matter which is of the greatest importance agriculturally, and that is the education of our farmers as far as it is possible to go in the way of encouraging them to adopt better methods of farming. We are doing this now through our fairs, our agricultural press and the splendid system of experimental farms throughout the Dominion.
I think we have one of the best systems of experimental farms to be found anywhere in the world. When I was across the water I visited some institutions of this character in Great Britain, but they did not have anything over there superior to our Central experiments farm.
Immigration, too, must receive attention. I believe in bringing in immigrants of the right kind, but I would close the door against Asiatics. As I come from British Columbia no one will want me to give reasons for their exclusion. It is sufficient to say that the Asiatic cannot assimilate with us and has a standard of living which makes it impossible for us to compete with him. But in bringing in immigrants we must secure those who will give promise of making good in this country. And when they get here we should not leave them alone, we should give them every assist [DOT] ance and through various institutions see that they derive full benefit from our assistance. I am not one of those who believe in bringing in immigrants indiscriminately and dumping them on the land. I believe in a vigorous immigration policy, but before we attempt to place any large number of immigrants on the land we should begin to put our own house in order. We can hardly expect the immigrant to remain with us if his neighbours tell him they are not making a dollar out of their farming; such a doleful tale will make him anxious to cross the line into the United States. I think the farmer in many instances has just cause of complaint in large sections of our country owing to conditions that have prevailed during recent years. Therefore I think we should improve conditions and particularly develop his market, because there is no better method of helping a farmer than the assurance that after he has his goods produced he can sell them at a profit.

The hon. member for Victoria City is opposed to oriental immigration because he comes from British Columbia, and one would naturally expect that. Well, I come from the prairie provinces, and naturally I am opposed to protection. Protection means that the farmer is working under a double standard, one standard to sell his goods by and another to purchase by. If the prairie provinces were not blessed with such fertile soil, such abundant sunshine and such favourable weather conditions, if it were not naturally a good country, the farmers could not possibly succeed under that condition of a double standard. We sell in competition with the world, our market is on the other side of the Atlantic. 
We grow the finest wheat grown anywhere in the world except in part of the United States and part of Russia. On the other hand, we purchase in what is known as the dearest country to live in. It is not many years ago you could ship freight on the Canadian National railway, and send it right through, whether it was going on the Canadian National or Canadian Pacific, by paying a transfer fee of $5 and getting a through rate. But since the freight rates have been advanced that privilege has been cut off. If you bill the freight on the Canadian National and ship it part way on that road and part way on the Canadian Pacific or vice versa, you have to pay two local freights, and it makes it absolutely prohibitive. This is something the Minister of Railways should certainly give his attention to, because if one railway will right this matter the other will have to follow suit and considering that the people of Canada own one of the large railways, it is right they should give the people a square deal.
Then express rates need looking after as well. I am sorry that I have to give you a

personal experience, but I want to explain to you what I mean when I speak of these express companies taking the money out of the people's pocket when carrying their goods. Last fall I had occasion to get a 2-inch coupling weighing about a pound. It was worth 30 cents in Winnipeg. However, I asked the merchant to send it C.O.L). because he would be sure to get his money. It had to be carried 85 miles on the railway, the express rate was 45 cents, and the C.O.D. for sending back the money was 25 cents. That made 70 cents for the carriage of this article worth 30 cents. Express rates are absolutely prohibitive.
Then labour costs are handicapping the western farmer very badly, not exactly the wages of the men engaged in agriculture, because they are not paid any too much, but the wages of the men engaged in manufacturing and the wag^s of the skilled artisans who are doing the work for the fanner. They are out of line absolutely with the price the farmer can get for his produce. If any one of us who are farming wanted to engage the services of a man with only a trowel, to pile up one brick on top of another, we would have to pay $10 a day and board. But take the other case. Suppose we went with a plough and four horses to work for him. He would allow us $3 a day for the man, $1 per day for each horse, and nothing for the plough, and consequently the labourer or artisan would receive $10 a day and the farmer would simply get $7 which is the rate of pay for man and team work.
This is taking away too much of the farmer's profits altogether. I will give an example of how this works out. I take this from the Breeders' Gazette, a paper that stands absolutely for the rights of the farmer in the United States. This matter was taken up only about six months ago by the editor of the Breeders' Gazette, Mr. Alvin Sanders. He mentioned the case of a brakeman who was working on a short run about 25 miles out of Chicago and back again, one train a day. This coloured brakeman was getting $250 a month. Close to this short line of railway were men working on the farms at $25 a. month. Why the difference? These men who were furnishing the freight to keep that railway alive were working for $25 a month, whereas the brakeman on the railway was drawing $250 a month. Such wages are absolutely out of line and they will have to be cut.
Another matter that we must take into consideration is that the labourer cannot work for small wages because the cost of living is

so high, and the reason for that high cost is the protective tariff. The distribution system in this country is absolutely out of line somehow or another, and the men and women who are selling their labour have to pay absolutely too high prices for the necessaries of life. Last fall the price for choice beef on the hoof in southern Manitoba was something like 4 cents per pound.
I sold steers for something like that price. If I had kept my steers over winter, I would have been docked in price because they would have weighed nearly 1,500 pounds apiece, so I sold them in the fall. That beef was worth on the hoof 8 cents per pound, and the hide and the offal would pay for the killing. That beef should have been sold at about 10 cents per pound, but I am quite prepared to say that the labouring man in Winnipeg paid nearly 30 cents per pound for it and for other things accordingly. The article states:
We have kicked with all the power at our command against the freight rates that have eaten up farmers and stockmen of various communities. We have kicked time and again at the unwillingness of labour to accept its due share in the great deflation. I should like to bring to the attention of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Fielding) a matter in connection with the stamp tax on cheques. WTe know a tax of 2 cents was put on cheques as a war measure a few years ago; but last year when the budget was first brought down, that tax was raised so that it was 2 cents for every $50, or 4 cents per $100, without any limit. Before the budget debate was over, the Minister of Finance announced that he was going to allow the stamp tax to be 2 cents for every $50 up to $5,000, but that then it was going to stop. That looked
to everyone very much as if the Minister of Finance were catering to the big interests, to those who do big business and pay money in large amounts. This year the stamp tax has been reduced. It is still 2 cents for every $50, but it stops at $2,500, and $1 is the maximum tax. That means simply that the tax on cheques is costing the common people .8 per cent. As a rule cheques issued by ordinary, common, everyday people would average about $25, so that they are paying .8 per cent for the privilege of issuing a cheque. On the other hand, cheques of corporations would average about $5,000, and in that case they are going to pay about .2 per cent. Thus in the one case, in the case of the wealthy corporation, .2 per cent is being paid, whereas in the case of the ordinary, everyday people, they are paying .8 per cent for the privilege of stamping their cheques. In other words, the business people are paying less than the working people. This stamp tax is rather a hardship from the fact that it was found by those who were dealing with large corporations in the city of Winnipeg last year, for instance, farmers selling cars of grain, that they always had to pay the price of that tax on cheques. This was brought to my notice even before the grain began to move, from the fact that live stock shippers ran up against that proposition in Winnipeg. One man especially who drew out $15,000 of his own money and went out to Alberta to buy cattle, found that he had to stamp his cheques before he drew out that $15,000 in Winnipeg. As he could not carry that money throughout Alberta around the different ranches, he had to put it into a bank in Alberta, and he issued cheques on that in payment of the stock he bought. That was twice he had to stamp his cheques. When he took his cattle to Winnipeg he was again charged for the stamps on the cheques by those to whom he sold the cattle. There was great dissatisfaction on account of this proposition, and I for one wrote to the Department of Finance to see if that could not be remedied. The Minister of Finance at that time was in Europe and the answer did not come from him; the answer from the department was to the effect that the law was fixed that all cheques had to be stamped, but the Finance Department did not care who stamped the cheques.

If anyone looks at the map of Canada and views that great big inland sea that comes right into the heart of the continent of North America, if he can conscientiously say that that great ocean highway was placed there by the Creator for no reason at all, I differ with him entirely. The great Liberal chieftain, Sir Wilfrid Laurier, used to say that the nineteenth century was the United States' growing time, but the twentieth century was going to be the growing time for Canada.
It is reasonable to imagine that the population of the United States is going to grow during the next fifty years as much as it has grown during the past half a century, and therefore she will be looking for an outlet for her surplus population long before the expiration of another fifty years. Fifty years is quite a long time in the life of an individual, but it is veryr short in the life of a nation. If the United States has to find more room for her surplus population where is she going to turn her eyes but to Canada? I have vision enought to realize that before fifty years have

elapsed not only will there be twenty million people in Canada but fifty million, and every seaport, including Vancouver, Prince Rupert, Port Nelson, Montreal, Quebec, Halifax and St. John, will be used to their full capacity.
To those who doubt whether the Hudson Bay railway is going to be profitable-and I know there are a good many doubters, more especially from eastern Canada-I should like to put up this proposition: If you are doubtful about the Hudson Bay railway and the route through the Straits being a workable proposition, just get behind us in our efforts to have the British preference increased to 100 per cent of the general tariff, and so bring all commodities which would then come from England duty free into the western country through the Hudson Bay route. I venture to say that if you do that the route will be in use six months in every year as soon as the railway is completed. The ships engaged on this route would then be able to carry cargoes both ways. One of the objections now urged against the feasibility of this route is that ships cannot get return cargoes. But if the British preference was extended to 100 per cent, every ship would be loaded to capacity both ways.

Now, whether we are agreeable to this proposition or not, I honestly believe that time will come when it will have to be taken in hand. The United States has nearly all the money of the world to-day, and consequently the other nations cannot purchase her commodities from lack of money, and she as a nation does not want to take goods from other nations in exchange for fear of causing unemployment at home. Consequently she is handicapped.
If the other nations of the world had more money and the United States had less, why, certainly trade would be in a better condition all round. Failing the realization of that proposition, Mr. Speaker, there is still another

proposition that I should like to put forward. It is not nearly as complicated and may therefore appeal to this House. In pursuance of my intention I shall place before the House an extract from The Times of February 23, 1923, being part of an address delivered by Sir George Lawson Johnston in the city of London on the preceding day.
I am not going to quote his address in full, but in order that hon. members may get the sense of what I am about to quote I shall have to read a greater portion of the address than I would otherwise do. Dealing with the burden of the American debt as it affects Great Britain he said:
Apparently the repayment of the war debt to America was to be an important factor in their taxation for the next sixty years.
When he saw them last February he had just returned from the States, and he mentioned to them how seriously our debt position had been worsened owing to Congress having by law fixed the period of repayment and the interest. Unfortunately, bankers, financiers, and others had talked so much about the capital and interest aspect of this debt, as if it were purely a business transaction, that a business atmosphere, instead of that associated with a debt of honour -on which nobody expects interest-had been created. As the business mind predominates on the other side of the Atlantic, once the matter had been fixed in the American mind as a business deal, it became impossible for our negotiators, no matttr how capable, to save the position. The most serious factor in the matter as now arranged is that we must pay capital and interest in United States dollars. It was generally admitted that the improvement in exchange from the British sovereign point of view duiing the last year was not so much on account of an improved trade balance as on account of American purchases of British securities. Such securities, if interest bearing, must eventually mean still further sums going from this country to the United States. There could be little doubt that efforts to pay America by direct remittance would turn exchange against us and seriously increase the number of pounds we should have to pay per annum, and, unfortunately, it would be just during our worst period of depression and bad trade that we should have to pay most pounds to buy the dollars.
A Dollar Reserve in Canada He would like to put forward a suggestion which might assist in this matter. It was that we should build up in Canada a reserve towards the payment of the American debt. The Canadian and United States dollars were not likely to vary seriously in value, therefore any fund we could build up in the Dominion would be comparatively free from exchange fluctuations. Canada was capable of being developed at a much more rapid pace than the present capital and man power at its lisposal could develop it. Our government could now borrow' at a lower rate than it had been able to do for a good many years. If it could obtain grants of land from Canada, it could utilize, say, one hundred million pounds in developing wheat areas, and probably certain industries in that Dominion; and this work, in conjunction with some considerable emigration scheme of selected unemployed, should develop in Canada a reproductive asset that would, after a while, annually supply dollars towards the payment to the States. Furthermore, every bushel of wheat bought from Canada instead of from the States would help to keep our exchange better with the latter.
We might thus accelerate the pace at which Canada was growing strong, and, at the same time, build up an asset that would much reduce the burden of the American debt, and probably, in the process, some of the money wre provided would purchase from our manufacturers agricultural implements and other machinery, etc.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that the British nation always keeps in mind that it must sell as well as purchase. We need also to keep that in mind.
His own experience in Canada convinced him that any such scheme to be successful would have to be planned and brought forward bv Canadians to meet their own views as regards the directions in which development should take place. If it was put forward at present they could feel, at any rate, that Canadian conditions would be understood Dy a British Premier who was bom in Canada, and a Colonial Secretary who had recently served as Governor-General.
I am putting forward that proposition because I think there is a great deal in it. Canada certainly needs more capital and more people to develop her natural resources. And, Sir, although I am going to vote against the budget because it is a protectionist budget, at the same time I may say that, although I was not born in Canada, I am a Canadian at heart and wish the country well, for it has done well by me.

the principal cause of voluntary sterility and race suicide in this country. The second point I wish to discuss is the unjust enactment or ruling of the taxation department regarding those who are married under the regime of community of property. This regime, I believe, exists only in the province of Quebec. Under our civil code persons can be married under the regime of community of property or under the regime of separation of property. If they are married without contract they fall under the regime of community of property. Now, subsection 3 of section 4 of the Income Tax Act passed in 1917, reads as follows:
Any persons carrying on business in partnership shall be liable for the income tax only in their individual capacity.
Discussion arose as to whether this section covered the case of a husband and wife married under the regime of community of property and whether they could separate their incomes for taxation purposes. Most of the legal authorities admitted that this was the right point of view, namely, that they could separate their incomes for taxation purposes. But in 1919 an amendment was passed and the law now reads as follows:
Subsection 3 of section 4 of the said act is repealed and the following is substituted therefor:
Any persons carrying on business in partnership shall be liable for the income tax only in their individual capacity; provided, however, that a husband and wife carrying on business together shall be deemed to be partners for any purpose under this Act.
The result is that a couple married under the regime of separation as to property pay much less than a couple married under the regime of community of property. Let me illustrate by an example. We will take two

The Budget-Mr. Archambault
couples without children whose income is $6,000. The first couple, we will say, are married under the regime of community of property; the husband has a salary of $3,000 and the wife has an income of $3,000. They are exempted up to only $2,000, leaving $4,000 on which they pay 4 per cent, or $160. The second couple are married under the regime of separation as to property; the husband earns a salary of $3,000, and his wife has an income of $3,000 the same as the first couple. The husband has an exemption of $2,000, and the wife also has an exemption of $2,000. Therefore they only pay a tax on $2,000, or only the sum of $80, while the other couple married under the regime of community of property pay the sum of $160. I say, Mr. Speaker, that that ruling is absolutely unjust and unfair, and I hope that the Minister of Finance on consideration will make a change in the law in order to put these two couples, whether married under the regime of community of property or separation, on the same plane for taxation purposes.
The third question which I desire to bring before the House is the differentiation between earned and unearned income for the purpose of taxation. I have had a resolution on the order paper regarding this matter for some time, but unfortunately it was not reached, and I therefore take this opportunity of discussing it now.
I may say, Mr. Speaker, that this differentiation exists in England and in order that this distinction may be thoroughly understood I will give the definition in the English law regarding earned and unearned income;
The expression "earned income" means-
Profits of office.-Any income arising in respect of any office or employment of profit held by the individual.
Pensions.-Income in respect of any pension, superannuation, or other allowance, deferred pay, or compensation for loss of office given in respect of the past services of the individual or of the husband or parent of the individual in any office or employment of profit, whether the individual or husband or parent of the individual shall have contributed to such pension, superannuation allowance, or deferred pay or not.
Property emoluments of office.-Any income from any property which is attached to or forms part of the emoluments of any office or employment of profit held by the individual.
Any income derived from farms.
Any income derived from a profession or trade.
There are some further particulars which are not so important. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that this legislation is very commendable. I believe, Mr. Speaker, that the man who derives his income from his own work, from his trade or profession, should not be asked to pay as high an income tax as the one who derives it from money that he has invested or
from money that he has inherited from his family.

Hear, hear.
Mr. ARCHAMBAULT; When the individual who works and earns his salary spends that salary, he spehds his own capital, and when he dies, if he has made just enough during his lifetime to enable him to support his wife and children, they are left without a cent, while in the case of the other man who has a large income from an inheritance or from money that he has succeeded in putting aside, when he dies his wife and children are left with both capital and income. But I also believe on the other hand that a fair re-apportionment and re-adjustment of the income tax would bring about a friendlier spirit between the wealthy, who are willing to be fair, and the less fortunate who would then realize that they are not victimized or overburdened. As I said in rising, my only purpose was to discuss some aspects of the income tax. I believe I have put my case as well as I can before the House and the minister, and I hope that he will take into consideration the few principles that I have dealt with and embody them into the bill which he will bring before the House later on the income tax.

The hour is late, and I have to catch a train in about two minutes, but as I look at the clock I realize that we are under what we call daylight saving, and I still have a few minutes to spare. I am not so sure, Mr. Speaker, but that the situation in which I am placed at the present moment might be made use of by the whips of the different groups in this House on certain occasions. For instance, the next time the hon. Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Motherwell) is going to address this House, it might be well for the chief whip of the government party to see that he is situated somewhat as I am at the present time. It might be well for the Conservative whip to see to it that when the hon. member for South Oxford (Mr. Sutherland), and the hon. member for North Toronto (Mr. Church) are billed to speak, they too have a pressing engagement somewhere shortly after they start. The shepherd of our own flock might, perhaps, work out this idea on the hon. member for Strathcona (Mr. Warner) or, perhaps,
better still the hon. member for Assiniboia (Mr. Gould).
I listened with a great deal of interest and pleasure the day before yesterday to the address given by the hon. member for Brantford (Mr. Raymond) and I always enjoy listening to him. His genial, humorous manner appeals to me, but I had some small degree of sympathy for him. I felt he was in somewhat of an awkward situation. He told the House this budget under discussion was satisfactory to him because of the fact that the ex-Minister of Finance (Sir Henry Drayton) could not find much fault with it. It appeared strange to me that almost the only argument which the Liberals presented in support of this budget was the fact that the chief critic of the Conservative party could not find very much fault with it. It appears to me, Mr. Speaker, that the days of the millennium must have arrived, and the lion and the lamb have surely lain down together.
Which is the lamb?

I rather think the lion is inside the lamb. I listened with very much interest and pleasure to the speech of the Minister of the Interior (Mr. Stewart). I have a great deal of admiration for the hon. member, but he also aroused my sympathy. He has not altogether fallen from grace, as he said yseterday:
I do not believe and I have had nothing to convince me that so heavy a rate of protection is required as is given to the industries existent in this country to-day.
I for one want to know definitely why such high protection is needed for some of these industries.
With both of these statements I can respond with a hearty "Amen." A peculiar situation exists at the present time. I claim, Sir, that I am a Liberal. That statement may perhaps cost me some votes if I ever find it necessary to look for votes again.
It surely will.

What I want to tell this House-and I hope my voice will go further than this House-is that as I understand Liberalism I still am a Liberal. Up to the present moment I cannot find myself guilty of having ever gone back upon what I was brought up to believe were true Liberal principles, but if I were to support this budget I am afraid my sleep would be disturbed for a good many nights to come. I was very much pleased with the speech which we listened to a few minutes ago by the hon. member who just sat down (Mr. Archambault). I have not the slightest doubt that he was more pleasantly and more genially employed in delivering a

The Budget-Mr. Findlay

speech of that kind than he would be in attempting to defend this budget. His speech was along Liberal lines,-fairly good Liberalism. I regret very much that I did not have an opportunity this afternoon of hearing all of the address of the hon. member for North Waterloo (Mr. Euler). I was very much impressed with the part I did hear. It was delivered in a fair and genial manner, but he too appeared to be in a peculiar situation. He made a speedy attempt to defend the tariff proposals but I could not help thinking of the days gone by when he and many more members sitting on the government benches to-day used to attack and condemn these very same tariff proposals, and I wondered why it was that to-day we find men who, a few years ago, were very emphatic and very energetic in their condemnation of the system of protec-titon, to-day defending a budget which they cannot but admit is a protective budget.
The hon. member says that I used to attack and condemn proposals such as are in the budget. Will he quote statements of mine to that effect?

I do not know that I can recall any particular instance, but I think I am not out of the way in saying that the hon. member as a Liberal has in tfie past opposed the protective tariff? Is that not correct?
I want for a few moments to refer to the amendment proposed by my honoured leader (Mr. Forke). It is charged that this amendment was carefully worded in order that it might not get the government into trouble. The duty of the group sitting in this section of the House is neither to get the government into trouble, nor to get the government out of trouble. As I understand our business, it is to endeavour to get good legislation, and personally I have never yet been prompted by any desire to get this government out of trouble. I must confess that I had some hopes; I was buoyed up with a good deal of hope that we might be able, by some means or another, to get something in the way of tariff reduction, relief from taxation, from this so-called Liberal government. You know it is said that "hope deferred maketh the heart sick." Sometimes it also makes it rebellious, and the time may come when we may be prompted, perhaps from a spirit of revenge, to join our forces even with the Conservative group from which we have no hopes of getting anything. We may, however, be tempted, from a motive of revenge, to join our forces with the gentlemen who sit to our right.	[DOT]

Oh, no.
Mr. Findlay.]

You are driving us to that. That may be the only course that is left open to us, and we may some time in the near future be compelled to take that course.
I was on the verge of saying that I could not help, the evening before last, drawing a comparison between some of the speeches that were made in this chamber. It is an unfortunate circumstance that it sometimes happens that a really good speech is postponed until the late hours of the night.
Oh, oh.

I am not saying that that has happened to-night by any means, but it did happen the night before last. During the afternoon and the early hours of the evening, a fairly well-filled chamber and a crowded gallery listened to a sort of burlesque on parliamentary procedure. Late in the night, when most people had gone home, a well thought-out, careful and sensible speech was delivered and almost lost on an empty house. That was an unfortunate occurrence. I only wish that I could bring before this House at least one of the thoughts that were presented to this Chamber by the hon. member for Nelson (Mr. Bird) the other evening. He was endeavouring to show how this movement in which we are engaged was a movement which was permanent, a movement which had come to stay, a movement which could not be injured because of ridicule hurled at the party in this House who are representing and supporting it. He said that the movement was greater than we are; that it would live after we were all gone; that even those who had been with it temporarily and who had gone back to the fleshpots could not but feel for a long time afterwards the exhilaration which they had received while amongst us. That thought I want to convey particularly to the hon. member for Muskoka (Mr. Hammell). When I use the prefix "honourable", I would like the Press Gallery and the Official Reporters to understand that an interrogation mark should come after that prefix, or my real meaning may not be conveyed to the country.
I am very much disappointed in the budget which has been presented to the House by a Liberal government. I have been a Liberal all my life. I supported Liberal principles because I believed in them, and I had hopes of this government which was elected on a platform containing planks in regard to their trade policy which I approved, which I believe a large number of the people of Canada approved, and which were largely responsible for putting this government into

Labour and Organization
power. There is not the slightest doubt that many people, especially in Ontario, were deceived by the trade planks of the Liberal platform of 1919, which planks this government since coming into power have repudiated. The time will come when the people will again have an opportunity to express themselves at the polls. As was said this evening, when this government have cut themselves loose, openly and above board from their platform of 1919, the people of Ontario and, indeed, the people of the whole of Canada from one end to the other will know exactly where the government stand. The next time they will appeal to the people, the people will understand perfectly that they can expect nothing in the way of tariff reduction or in the way of Liberal principles from the government which occupy the treasury benches at the present time.
